name: Resection Planning and Margins
title: Resection Planning and Margins
answer: Resection planning and margins covers the use of AI to define the tissue to be removed and the healthy border around it before and during surgery. This includes segmenting tumors and critical structures from preoperative CT, MRI, or PET scans, computing the planned resection volume, and updating that plan as the patient's anatomy shifts. The work spans neurosurgery, orthopedic oncology, liver and lung resection, and other fields where a negative margin is a primary goal.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Resection planning and margins covers the use of AI to define the tissue to be removed and the healthy border around it before and during surgery. This includes segmenting tumors and critical structures from preoperative CT, MRI, or PET scans, computing the planned resection volume, and updating that plan as the patient's anatomy shifts. The work spans neurosurgery, orthopedic oncology, liver and lung resection, and other fields where a negative margin is a primary goal.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on hospital imaging archives and surgical navigation workstations, often linked to robotic arms or instrument trackers. Preoperative planning may use GPU-equipped servers for segmentation and registration, while intraoperative use relies on lower-latency local compute near the operating room. Inputs include preoperative volumetric scans, intraoperative ultrasound or cone-beam CT, and optical or electromagnetic tracking data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is image segmentation, where a model labels tumor, organ, and at-risk structures, followed by deformable registration to align the preoperative plan with the patient on the table. Margin distance is then computed as a three-dimensional safety buffer around the tumor boundary, and the plan is displayed as a colored overlay on navigation screens. Some systems also analyze frozen section or ex vivo specimen images to estimate whether the cut surface is clear of tumor.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Patient imaging data used for planning is subject to health privacy rules, and the training data behind a model must be documented for provenance and population fit. A wrong margin can lead to recurrence or avoidable loss of function, so surgeons remain responsible for final resection decisions and must be able to override any AI suggestion. Regulatory clearance usually requires evidence that the tool does not increase positive margin rates or harm, and product liability questions remain active in this area.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward real-time margin assessment during the cut, using optical imaging, mass spectrometry, or rapid tissue analysis to tell the surgeon whether more tissue must be removed. Augmented reality overlays are likely to merge the planned margin with the live surgical field, and robotic systems may take on constrained sub-tasks such as holding a plane or pausing at a margin boundary. Personalized margins based on tumor genomics and recurrence risk are also being explored.
